section.heading: 8.8. Applications of Double Integrals
section.paragraph: In this section, we will discuss applications involving the double integral.
section.heading: Finding the Volume of a Solid by Double Integrals
section.paragraph: As we saw earlier, the double integral
gives the volume of the solid bounded by the graph of $$f\left( {x,y} \right)$$ over the region $$R$$ .

note.source_type: The Volume of a Solid Under a Surface
note.title: The Volume of a Solid Under a Surface
note.heading: The Volume of a Solid Under a Surface
note.paragraph: Let $$R$$ be a region in the $$\mathit{xy}$$ -plane and let $$f$$ be continuous and nonnegative on $$R$$ . Then, the volume of a solid under a surface bounded above by $$z = f\left( {x,y} \right)$$ and below by $$R$$ is given by
$$V = {\int_{R}{\int{f\left( {x,y} \right)dA}}}$$

section.heading: Population of a City
section.paragraph: Suppose the plane region $$R$$ represents a certain district of a city and $$f\left( {x,y} \right)$$ gives the population density (the number of people per square mile) at any point $$\left( {x,y} \right)$$ in $$R$$ . Enclose the set $$R$$ by a rectangle, and construct a grid for it in the usual manner. In any rectangular region of the grid that has no point in common with $$R$$ , set $$f\left( {x_{i},y_{i}} \right)hk = 0$$ (Figure 42). Then, corresponding to any grid covering the set $$R$$ , the general term of the Riemann sum $$f\left( {x_{i},y_{i}} \right)hk$$ (population density times area) gives the number of people living in that part of the city corresponding to the rectangular region $$R_{i}$$ . Therefore, the Riemann sum gives an approximation of the number of people living in the district represented by $$R$$ and, in the limit, the double integral
gives the actual number of people living in the district under consideration.

section.heading: Average Value of a Function
section.paragraph: In Section 6.5, we showed that the average value of a continuous function $$f(x)$$ over an interval $$\left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack$$ is given by

That is, the average value of a function over $$\left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack$$ is the integral of $$f$$ over $$\left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack$$ divided by the length of the interval. An analogous result holds for a function of two variables $$f\left( {x,y} \right)$$ over a plane region $$R$$ . To see this, we enclose $$R$$ by a rectangle and construct a rectangular grid. Let $$\left( {x_{i},y_{i}} \right)$$ be any point in the rectangle $$R_{i}$$ of area $$hk$$ . Now, the average value of the $$mn$$ numbers $${f\left( {x_{1},y_{1}} \right)},{f\left( {x_{2},y_{2}} \right)},\ldots,{f\left( {x_{mn},y_{mn}} \right)}$$ is given by

Now the area of $$R$$ is approximated by the sum of the $$mn$$ rectangles (omitting those having no points in common with $$R$$ ), each of area $$hk$$ . Note that this is the denominator of the previous expression. Therefore, taking the limit as $$m$$ and $$n$$ both tend to infinity, we obtain the following formula for the average value of $$f\left( {x,y} \right)$$ over $$R$$ .

note.source_type: Average Value of f ( x , y ) over the Region R
note.title: Average Value of f ( x , y ) over the Region R
note.heading: Average Value of f ( x , y ) over the Region R
note.paragraph: If $$f$$ is integrable over the plane region $$R$$ , then its average value over $$R$$ is given by
$$\frac{\int_{R}{\int{f(x,y)dA}}}{ \text{Area} {of}R}$$
or
$$\frac{\int_{R}{\int{f(x,y)dA}}}{\int_{R}{\int{dA}}}$$

note.title: Notes
note.heading: Notes
note.paragraph: If we let $$f\left( {x,y} \right) = 1$$ for all $$\left( {x,y} \right)$$ in $$R$$ , then
$$\int_{R}{\int{f\left( {x,y} \right)dA = {\int_{R}{\int{dA = {Area of}R}}}}}$$
